direct_answer:
Aker BP states that it conducted a double materiality assessment (DMA) using a systematic, structured process to identify material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) and the associated sustainability matters for reporting, covering both (i) impact materiality (inside-out: impacts from its activities on environment and society) and (ii) financial materiality (outside-in: financial risks and opportunities sustainability issues pose to its business model and performance, including reputational risk and dependencies on natural, human and social resources) [Source 1]. The DMA was revised in 2024 based on new information, implementation guidance and EFRAG’s draft oil and gas sector standard, and included mapping IROs, their dependencies, and their connection to Aker BP’s own operations and value chain [Source 4]. Aker BP considered activities, business relationships and geographies when evaluating potential IROs; it focused on oil and gas production for own-operations materiality, development projects for upstream value chain materiality, and noted downstream impacts related to the use of petroleum products [Source 3].

Stakeholder engagement was used to identify risks, opportunities and actual/potential impacts, including public consultations for PDO impact assessments (with reports shared with “over 40 key stakeholders”), publication of impact assessments, and a whistleblowing channel for concerns [Source 2]. Aker BP says it included stakeholders’ perspectives and priorities in the DMA; in 2024 this was achieved through in-depth interviews and workshops with internal management and subject matter experts, and the process was based on prior-year interviews involving owners, key suppliers, customers, NGOs and authorities [Source 2].

For assessment and prioritisation, Aker BP applied severity x likelihood ratings for IROs (aligned with its enterprise risk management approach using company scales and a shared risk matrix) and gave “special attention” to dependencies between impacts and related risks/opportunities; IROs are documented in the same tool as other company risks and prioritised/handled together [Source 1]. The DMA is described as iterative: defining business context (activities, business model, value chain, stakeholders, boundaries), identifying actual and potential IROs using top-down and bottom-up approaches with internal/external stakeholder input and quantitative sources, assessing/prioritising based on impact and financial materiality criteria using a standardised rating system, and validating outcomes by management and the Board with ongoing monitoring/updates [Source 7]. Aker BP also links its sustainability due diligence (OECD-based, risk-based, covering supply chain and other business relationships and embedded into business processes) to identifying and assessing adverse impacts, referencing the DMA as the place where adverse impacts are identified and assessed [Source 8].

Sustainability matters identified as material from both an impact and a financial perspective (i.e., high impact and high financial relevance / “strategic and highest priority”) are: climate change, own workforce, pollution, business conduct, and resource use and circular economy [Source 3].
compliance_rationale: The passages provide clear evidence that Aker BP performed a DMA covering both impact and financial materiality, considered value chain and dependencies, used severity x likelihood scoring aligned to ERM, and incorporated stakeholder perspectives through multiple channels with Board/management validation [Sources 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8]. The material matters that are material from both perspectives are explicitly listed in the materiality matrix description [Source 3]. However, the retrieved passages do not provide the detailed thresholds/criteria definitions (e.g., severity dimensions such as scale/scope/irremediable character, or financial magnitude thresholds) nor a complete list of all material matters and IROs beyond the matrix summary, limiting full ESRS 1 alignment based on evidence provided.
disclosure_gaps: Explicit qualitative/quantitative thresholds used to determine materiality (beyond stating severity x likelihood scoring) are not provided in the retrieved passages [Sources 1, 7].

Detailed impact materiality criteria (e.g., how severity is broken down into scale, scope, irremediable character; and how likelihood is applied) are not evidenced in the retrieved passages [Source 1].

Detailed financial materiality criteria (e.g., how magnitude of financial effects is assessed and what constitutes ‘material’ financial effects) are not evidenced in the retrieved passages [Source 1].

A complete, itemised list of material IROs and which sustainability matters are material only for impact or only for financial materiality is not included in the retrieved passages (table 3 is referenced but not provided) [Source 6].

Evidence of direct engagement with affected stakeholders (as distinct from key stakeholder groups and internal interviews/workshops) in the 2024 DMA process is limited in the retrieved passages [Source 2].
Cross-matter effects/trade-offs (where actions on one matter create material impacts/risks in another) are not evidenced in the retrieved passages.
key_findings: DMA covers both impact (inside-out) and financial (outside-in) materiality, including reputational risk and dependencies on natural, human and social resources [Source 1].

2024 DMA is a revision of the first DMA conducted in 2023; it mapped IROs, dependencies and value chain connections and was updated using new information and guidance (including EFRAG draft oil & gas sector standard) [Source 4].

Assessment considers activities, business relationships and geographies; focuses on oil and gas production for own operations, development projects for upstream value chain, and acknowledges downstream impacts from use of petroleum products [Source 3].

Stakeholder engagement informs DMA via public consultations for PDO impact assessments, publication of impact assessments, whistleblowing channel, and interviews/workshops; prior-year interviews included owners, suppliers, customers, NGOs and authorities [Source 2].

IROs are assessed using severity x likelihood, aligned with enterprise risk management and prioritised together with other company risks; dependencies between impacts and risks/opportunities receive special attention [Source 1].
Material matters identified as material from both impact and financial perspectives: climate change, own workforce, pollution, business conduct, resource use and circular economy [Source 3].
